###### Abstract

Large language models have evolved from single-turn chatbots into
interactive agents capable of long-horizon reasoning. In real
deployments, MCP tool services can return noisy feedback and users may
intervene to correct the agent, but existing methods provide limited
supervision for reflection learning and failure recovery. To bridge this
gap, we propose Agent-Reflex, a general training framework for
incentivizing proactive reflection in agents. Specifically, Agent-Reflex
comprises three stages. First, Environment Reflection Skill Discovery
(RSD) injects grounded tool-feedback perturbations into environment
scaling, samples a capability-diverse LLM pool, mines matched
success–failure pairs, and summarizes reusable reflection meta-skills.
Building on this skill library, we then apply Reflective Supervised
Fine-Tuning (ReSFT) that converts each skill into supervision for
self-reflection, skill recovery, and user-centric correction,
strengthening complementary reflective behaviors. Finally, we propose
On-Policy Reflective Policy Optimization (ORPO) to combine agentic
reinforcement learning under noisy interactions with reflection-guided
on-policy distillation to further elicit proactive reflection. Built on
Qwen3-8B, Agent-Reflex reaches 58.6 overall on five long-horizon
tool-use benchmarks and 29.1 on AgentNoiseBench, surpassing strong
environment-scaling and reflection baselines. Experiments on six
challenging agent benchmark suites demonstrate the effectiveness of
Agent-Reflex. Further analyses show that Agent-Reflex improves agents’
robustness to noise while maintaining stable training dynamics,
supporting scalable agent training.

## 1 Introduction

Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have extended their
applications from natural language tasks to practical workflows that
require long-horizon reasoning ([Yao et al., 2023](#bib.bib1); [Patil et
al., 2025](#bib.bib2); [Trivedi et al., 2024](#bib.bib3); [Barres et
al., 2025](#bib.bib4); [Dong et al., 2026b](#bib.bib53)). Meeting this
demand requires agents not only to master tool interfaces but also to
accumulate transferable interaction experience from dynamic
environments. Building diverse, stateful environments that faithfully
capture real-world interaction logic has therefore become the foundation
for scaling agent capability.

Recent studies to scale agent training environments can be roughly
categorized into two groups. One group, exemplified by Simia ([Li et
al., 2025](#bib.bib5)) and GenEnv ([Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib6)),
treats LLMs as implicit textual world models that generate feedback from
tool specifications and interaction histories. These approaches
substantially reduce environmental engineering costs, but the feedback
generated can be hallucinated. Instead, a complementary family
explicitly reproduces real interaction logic, synthesizing executable
tools and environment databases: it extracts databases from real-world
service themes, generates executable tools, and synthesizes tasks with
verifiable results ([Song et al., 2026](#bib.bib7); [Wang et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib8); [Tu et al., 2026](#bib.bib9); [Dong et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib10)). As a result, these executable environments give
agents a basis for learning interaction patterns that transfer across
environments.

Although environment scaling improves interaction diversity and
out-of-distribution generalization, existing agent-training paradigms
still rely on an idealized assumption: agents interact with stable,
well-controlled environments under minimal user intervention. This
mismatch with real-world deployment reveals two inherent challenges (as
shown in
Figure [1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")):

(1) Lack of noisy feedback. Real-world tool services are unreliable,
frequently returning timeouts and service errors. Existing training
environments usually assume stable and noise-free feedback, leaving
agents underprepared for failure detection and recovery ([Wang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib17); [Gupta, 2026](#bib.bib46)).

(2) Lack of user-guided correction. Real users actively intervene when
an agent deviates from their intent, correcting its reasoning and
actions. Existing user simulators often rely on standardized templates,
with limited coverage of corrective instructions and diverse interaction
styles during execution ([Barres et al., 2025](#bib.bib4); [Qian et al.,
2025](#bib.bib51); [Suhr and Artzi, 2023](#bib.bib52)).

Together, these challenges reveal that agents still lack proactive
reflection under noisy external feedback. Ideally, a robust agent should
continuously perceive environmental noise, task failures, and user
correction intent, then promptly revise its actions. Existing reflection
methods explore inference-time reflection, correction-trajectory
learning, and noise-augmented training ([Shinn et al.,
2023](#bib.bib11); [Madaan et al., 2023](#bib.bib12); [Yuan et al.,
2025](#bib.bib13); [Bi et al., 2026](#bib.bib14); [Zhang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib15); [Chen et al., 2026](#bib.bib16)), but most are
trained in stateless or simplified environments, leaving one question
open: _How can we elicit proactive reflective capability in agents from
execution failures in real-world environments?_

To address this gap, we propose Agent-Reflex, a general training
framework for incentivizing proactive reflective thinking in agents. It
models reflection as a learnable meta-skill: transferable meta-skills
are explicitly mined from execution failures and progressively
internalized into the policy through verifiable reflection learning.
Specifically, Agent-Reflex comprises three components:

(1) Environment Reflection Skill Discovery (RSD). We anchor 557
high-usage real-world environment themes and automatically construct
database-backed executable environments and tasks, injecting diverse
tool-return failures to emulate noisy conditions. From a diverse LLM
agent pool, we sample trajectories covering varied task types and
response styles, and matched success/failure pairs are then mined into
1,170 reflection meta-skills across 557 environments.

(2) Reflective Supervised Fine-Tuning (ReSFT). Given the skill library,
we design three auxiliary and verifiable reflection sampling strategies:
Self-Reflection (SR), Skill Recovery (KR), and User-Centric Reflection
(UR), which strengthen reflection at different levels. Supervised
fine-tuning then internalizes these explicit skills into the agent
policy.

(3) On-Policy Reflective Policy Optimization (ORPO). To further elicit
proactive reflection, ORPO combines Noisy Agent RL with
reflection-guided on-policy distillation. For each task we match its
environment’s reflection meta-skill and rollout in the noisy
environment, optimizing the policy by reinforcement learning from
verifiable rewards. The same action tokens are then re-scored under a
privileged skill context, and a confidence-weighted OPD objective ([Wu
et al., 2026](#bib.bib28)) turns this contrast into dense supervision
for reflection decisions.

Experiments on six long-horizon tool-use and noisy-interaction
benchmarks demonstrate the effectiveness of Agent-Reflex. Further
analysis shows that it improves noise robustness and keeps training
dynamics stable, supporting scalable general-agent training.

Therefore, our contributions are threefold:

- •
  We identify two gaps between idealized synthetic environments and
  real-world deployment in agent interaction, namely lack of noisy
  environment feedback and lack of user-guided correction during
  execution, highlighting the importance of reflection learning for
  noisy interactions.
- •
  We introduce RSD, which systematically builds a scalable
  noisy-environment ecosystem by incorporating real-tool perturbations
  and mining reflection meta-skills from large-scale success/ failure
  trajectory pairs sampled by an LLM Agent Pool.
- •
  We further propose ReSFT and ORPO. ReSFT builds multi-level reflection
  data through three sampling strategies and internalizes it by
  supervised fine-tuning; ORPO adds reflection-guided on-policy
  distillation to Noisy Agent RL for token-level supervision of failed
  executions.

## 2 Related Work

Agent Reflection Learning. Agent reflection differs in where the
corrective signal lives. Inference-time methods leave parameters
untouched: Reflexion and Self-Refine append a verbal self-critique, and
ExpeL retrieves cross-task insights at test time ([Shinn et al.,
2023](#bib.bib11); [Madaan et al., 2023](#bib.bib12); [Zhao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib30)). Because the critique comes from the policy that
failed, a well-formed but wrong tool return is rarely contradicted.
Training-time methods move the signal into a per-trajectory repair:
Agent-R, ReflectRL, and LoongReflect learn from that repair ([Yuan et
al., 2025](#bib.bib13); [Bi et al., 2026](#bib.bib14); [Zhang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib15)), and NoisyAgent exposes the policy to perturbed
interaction under only a scalar return ([Chen et al.,
2026](#bib.bib16)). Either way, nothing accumulates into an
environment-level statement a later episode can reuse. Agent-Reflex
mines cross-model success/failure contrasts under the same injected
noise into environment-indexed meta-skills and internalizes them through
two-stage training.

Scalable Environment Synthesis for Agent Training. Diverse, stateful
environments underpin tool use and long-horizon decision making. One
line of work simulates interaction feedback with language models,
treating tool specifications and dialogue history as an implicit world
model ([Li et al., 2025](#bib.bib5); [Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib6)). A
second makes the environment itself executable: EnvScaler and ScaleEnv
synthesize tools with verifiable tasks ([Song et al., 2026](#bib.bib7);
[Tu et al., 2026](#bib.bib9)), Agent-World scales database-backed
services over hundreds of real-world themes and verifies outcomes
through state transitions ([Dong et al., 2026a](#bib.bib10); [Wang et
al., 2026b](#bib.bib8)), and EnvACE internalizes environment dynamics
through world rehearsal ([Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib23)). All of them
scale the _supply_ of solvable environments, whereas Agent-Reflex keeps
the database-backed paradigm but turns the failures inside those
environments into supervision, mining diagnosis and recovery rules from
cross-model success/failure contrasts under perturbations derived from
real tool errors.
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Supplement Related Work ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")
gives an extended discussion of reflection learning, environment
synthesis, and agentic RL.

## 3 Methodology: Agent-Reflex

Overview.
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 3 Methodology: Agent-Reflex ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")
summarizes the pipeline. To convert environment failures into a
reflection capability, Agent-Reflex comprises three stages:

(1) Environment Reflection Skill Discovery (RSD)
([§ 3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Stage 1: Environment Reflection Skill Discovery (RSD) ‣ 3 Methodology: Agent-Reflex ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")).
Build failure-aware executable environments and mine verifier-matched
pairs into an offline skill library.

(2) Reflective Supervised Fine-Tuning (ReSFT)
([§ 3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Stage 2: Reflective Supervised Fine-Tuning (ReSFT) ‣ 3 Methodology: Agent-Reflex ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")).
Convert each skill into verifier-validated self-reflection, recovery,
and user-correction data.

(3) On-Policy Reflective Policy Optimization (ORPO)
([§ 3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 Stage 3: On-Policy Reflective Policy Optimization (ORPO) ‣ 3 Methodology: Agent-Reflex ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")).
Combine Noisy Agent RL with same-token skill-guided OPD to provide dense
reflection supervision.

![Refer to caption](2610.17953v1/figure2_final.png)

Figure 2: RSD and ReSFT. Stage 1 perturbs tool returns of 557
MCP-anchored executable environments with mined failure families,
contrasting success/failure rollouts into an offline skill library.
Stage 2 samples local-repair (SR), global-recovery (KR), and
user-correction (UR) continuations from that library, keeping only
verifier-validated ones with skill prompts stripped.

### 3.1 Stage 1: Environment Reflection Skill Discovery (RSD)

#### 3.1.1 Noise-Grounded Environment Scaling

To construct realistic environments with tool failures, we select 557
high-usage MCP server specifications from Smithery¹¹ 1
[https://smithery.ai/](https://smithery.ai/), each defining an
environment topic $`m\in\mathcal{M}`$. Following Agent-World ([Dong et
al., 2026a](#bib.bib10)), a research agent equipped with search,
browser, coding, and operating-system tools builds and iteratively
enriches a topic-grounded database. A coding agent then generates
candidate tools and unit tests from each topic and its database. We
retain only tools that compile, pass all tests, satisfy state-transition
constraints, and support executable task verification. Thus, each
environment $`\mathcal{E}_{m}`$ consists of a database, a validated tool
set, and corresponding verifiers. The resulting ecosystem is
$`\mathcal{E}=\{\mathcal{E}_{m}:m\in\mathcal{M}\}`$, with 60
verifier-backed tasks per topic; the resulting task set $`\mathcal{Q}`$
supplies the ReSFT data.

Tool-Failure Mining and Injection. Because real deployment is unstable,
we ground perturbations in observed failures rather than invent them. We
replay agents across nine public agentic benchmarks whose environments
expose production-grade tool ecosystems and log every tool return
(Appendix [D.2](#A4.SS2 "D.2 Stage 1: Environment Construction and Skill Discovery ‣ Appendix D Implementation Details ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")).
In total we collect 177,700 tool returns, of which 24,510 are error
returns, and group them by surface form into eight actionable failure
families
(Table [4](#A4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ D.2 Stage 1: Environment Construction and Skill Discovery ‣ Appendix D Implementation Details ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")).
We then inject these failures into tool returns probabilistically to
emulate real deployment:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
o_{t+1}^{\mathrm{train}}=\begin{cases}J(o_{t+1}),&b_{t+1}^{\mathrm{inj}}=1,\\
o_{t+1},&b_{t+1}^{\mathrm{inj}}=0,\end{cases}\qquad b_{t+1}^{\mathrm{inj}}\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p_{\mathrm{inj}}),
``` |  | (1) |

where the renderer $`J`$ replaces the true return with a failure drawn
from those compatible with the invoked tool $`f_{t}`$, balanced across
the eight families so that rare ones still receive enough instances for
recovery to be learned. Here $`p_{\mathrm{inj}}`$ is the per-return
injection probability, and we keep clean and perturbed tasks only if
they admit a verifiable solution and recovery, respectively.

#### 3.1.2 Reflection Meta-Skill Extraction

Capability-Diverse Trajectory Sampling and Pairing. Repeated sampling
from one model can concentrate trajectories around its model-specific
reasoning tendencies ([Jiang et al., 2023](#bib.bib49); [Du et al.,
2024](#bib.bib50)). We therefore sample trajectories from a
capability-diverse LLM pool $`\Pi_{\mathrm{pool}}`$ of nine models
spanning five families, ranging from 4B to 284B parameters
(Table [5](#A4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ D.2 Stage 1: Environment Construction and Skill Discovery ‣ Appendix D Implementation Details ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")).
Each model interacts with the noisy ecosystem $`\mathcal{E}`$ on every
task $`q\in\mathcal{Q}`$ under the same sampling protocol.

Because rule-based metrics cannot reliably assess long-horizon
trajectories, an analyzer model and the environment verifier jointly
label each rollout, yielding
$`\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{correct}}=\{(q_{i},\tau_{i}^{+})\}_{i=1}^{N_{+}}`$
and
$`\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{error}}=\{(q_{i},\tau_{i}^{-},e_{i},t_{i}^{\star},s_{t_{i}^{\star}})\}_{i=1}^{N_{-}}`$,
where $`\tau_{i}^{+}`$ and $`\tau_{i}^{-}`$ denote correct and erroneous
trajectories, $`e_{i}`$ is the diagnosed error rationale,
$`t_{i}^{\star}`$ is the first erroneous turn, and $`s_{t_{i}^{\star}}`$
is its environment-state snapshot. We pair correct and erroneous
trajectories from the same task, limit the number of pairs contributed
by each task, and require each environment to draw pairs from at least
five distinct tasks, forming:
$`\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pair}}=\{(q,\tau^{+},\tau^{-},e,t^{\star},s_{t^{\star}})\}`$.

Meta-Skill Extraction. An ideal reflective meta-skill is an environment
recovery rule that maps an agent’s bad pattern to a corrective action,
enabling reuse across tasks within the same environment. To mine such
skills, an analyzer examines paired successful and failed trajectories,
identifies recurring failure patterns, and converts them into executable
recovery rules. For each environment $`m`$, we store
$`\zeta_{m}=(d_{m},\mathcal{T}_{m},\mathcal{B}_{m},\mathcal{K}_{m})`$,
where $`d_{m}`$ describes the environment and its business objects,
$`\mathcal{T}_{m}`$ its tools, $`\mathcal{B}_{m}`$ its observed bad
patterns, and $`\mathcal{K}_{m}`$ the extracted reflection skills. The
resulting offline library is
$`\mathcal{K}=\bigcup_{m\in\mathcal{M}}\mathcal{K}_{m}`$, so each sample
in $`\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{pair}}`$ is associated with a skill
$`\kappa\in\mathcal{K}_{m}`$. Representative environment-specific skills
are shown in
Appendix [E.3](#A5.SS3 "E.3 Representative Environment-Specific Skills ‣ Appendix E Supplement Experimental Results ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively").

### 3.2 Stage 2: Reflective Supervised Fine-Tuning (ReSFT)

ReSFT converts explicit reflection skills into policy behavior. Starting
from a frozen behavior policy $`\pi_{0}`$, we construct three
complementary forms of reflective supervision for local repair, global
recovery, and user-guided correction.

Self-Reflection Sampling (SR). For an erroneous trajectory $`\tau^{-}`$,
let $`t^{\star}`$ be its first erroneous turn, $`s_{t^{\star}}`$ the
environment-state snapshot taken before that turn is executed,
$`h_{t^{\star}}`$ the deployment-visible history up to that turn, and
$`\kappa`$ the matched reflection skill. Let $`x\oplus z`$ denote
appending $`z`$ to context $`x`$, and let
$`\operatorname{Ver}_{s}(x,y)`$ indicate whether continuation $`y`$
successfully completes the task after restoring the environment to state
$`s`$. To teach failure awareness and self-reflection, we restore the
environment to $`s_{t^{\star}}`$ and continue after appending the
corrective skill:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
y^{\mathrm{SR}}\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot\mid h_{t^{\star}}\oplus\kappa),\qquad\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{SR}}=\{(h_{t^{\star}},y^{\mathrm{SR}}):\operatorname{Ver}_{s_{t^{\star}}}(h_{t^{\star}},y^{\mathrm{SR}})=1\}.
``` |  | (2) |

The skill triggers diagnosis and replanning during generation but is
removed from the stored input, so the policy learns to recover from its
own error state.

Skill Recovery Sampling (KR). Many failures originate from an incorrect
initial plan rather than a local tool error. To teach global recovery,
we reset the environment to its initial state $`s_{0}`$ and restart from
the original task with the matched skill:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
y^{\mathrm{KR}}\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot\mid q\oplus\kappa),\qquad\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{KR}}=\{(q,y^{\mathrm{KR}}):\operatorname{Ver}_{s_{0}}(q,y^{\mathrm{KR}})=1\}.
``` |  | (3) |

As in SR, the privileged skill is removed before storage, encouraging
recovery without an explicit skill prior.

User-Centric Reflection Sampling (UR). When an agent deviates from the
user’s intent, users may intervene and correct its reasoning. To teach
user-centric reflection, a user simulator $`U`$ converts the matched
skill into a natural-language correction:
$`u_{\kappa}=U(\kappa,h_{t^{\star}},s_{t^{\star}})`$. We then restore
the environment to $`s_{t^{\star}}`$, insert the correction after the
erroneous turn, and continue:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
y^{\mathrm{UR}}\sim\pi_{0}(\cdot\mid h_{t^{\star}}\oplus u_{\kappa}),\qquad\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{UR}}=\{(h_{t^{\star}}\oplus u_{\kappa},y^{\mathrm{UR}}):\operatorname{Ver}_{s_{t^{\star}}}(h_{t^{\star}}\oplus u_{\kappa},y^{\mathrm{UR}})=1\}.
``` |  | (4) |

Because the user message is deployment-visible, $`u_{\kappa}`$ remains
in the stored input, whereas the privileged skill $`\kappa`$ is removed.

Let
$`\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{correct}}^{\pi_{0}}\subseteq\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{correct}}`$
denote correct trajectories generated by the target policy $`\pi_{0}`$.
We merge them with the three reflective datasets:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ReSFT}}=\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{correct}}^{\pi_{0}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{SR}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{KR}}\cup\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{UR}},\qquad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ReSFT}}=-\!\!\sum_{(x,y)\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{ReSFT}}}\log\pi_{\theta}(y\mid x).
``` |  | (5) |

### 3.3 Stage 3: On-Policy Reflective Policy Optimization (ORPO)

ReSFT provides an offline initialization by internalizing explicit
reflection skills. To further elicit proactive reflection from the
current policy on its own on-policy rollouts, ORPO supplements
outcome-based agentic reinforcement learning with token-level,
reflection-guided on-policy distillation (OPD) ([Agarwal et al.,
2024](#bib.bib47); [Zhao et al., 2026](#bib.bib48); [Wu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib28)), providing dense supervision for failure-causing
decisions.

![Refer to caption](2610.17953v1/Figure3_new.png)

Figure 3: ORPO. A mixed rollout group of mostly clean and a few
perturbed trajectories shares one group-normalized advantage. Re-scoring
the same tokens with and without the skill card of their environment
yields the detached, confidence-weighted OPD signal.

Noisy Agentic Reinforcement Learning. At update $`u`$, we draw a task
$`q`$ from the EnvScaler RL task pool
$`\mathcal{Q}_{\mathrm{RL}}`$ ([Song et al., 2026](#bib.bib7)), which
ORPO directly reuses instead of RSD-synthesized tasks, and construct one
mixed on-policy group to expose the behavior policy to noisy environment
feedback. Specifically, the policy $`\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}`$
generates $`G`$ trajectories
$`\mathcal{G}_{q}=\{\tau_{q}^{(i)}\}_{i=1}^{G}`$, with a fraction
$`\nu`$ rolled out in noisy environments and the remainder in clean
ones. All trajectories retain the complete tool interaction and final
answer, and none is given a reflection-skill prompt. After rollout, the
environment verifier assigns each trajectory a return $`R_{q,i}`$; we
normalize these returns within the mixed group:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mu_{q}=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}R_{q,i},\qquad\sigma_{q}^{2}=\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\bigl(R_{q,i}-\mu_{q}\bigr)^{2},\qquad\widehat{A}_{q,i}=\frac{R_{q,i}-\mu_{q}}{\sigma_{q}+\epsilon},
``` |  | (6) |

where normalizing over the mixed group rather than within its clean and
perturbed strata keeps genuine failures inside the on-policy
distribution without letting them form a contrast of their own. For an
agent action token $`a_{q,i,t,k}`$ at position $`k`$ of turn $`t`$ under
history $`h_{q,i,t}`$, we define the token log-probability of the
current policy and its ratio to the behavior policy:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\ell^{\theta}_{q,i,t,k}=\log\pi_{\theta}\bigl(a_{q,i,t,k}\mid h_{q,i,t},a_{q,i,t,<k}\bigr),\qquad\rho_{q,i,t,k}(\theta)=\exp\bigl(\ell^{\theta}_{q,i,t,k}-\ell^{\mathrm{old}}_{q,i,t,k}\bigr),
``` |  | (7) |

with $`\ell^{\mathrm{old}}`$ the same score under
$`\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}`$. Letting $`\chi_{q,i,t,k}\in\{0,1\}`$
mask the valid agent-generated tokens, which excludes tool returns and
simulated user messages, the clipped Agent RL objective is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RL}}(\theta)=-\,\mathbb{E}_{q,i,t,k}\Bigl[\chi_{q,i,t,k}\min\bigl(\rho_{q,i,t,k}\widehat{A}_{q,i},\ \operatorname{clip}(\rho_{q,i,t,k},1-\epsilon_{c},1+\epsilon_{c})\,\widehat{A}_{q,i}\bigr)\Bigr]\\
+\beta_{\mathrm{KL}}\,\mathbb{E}_{h\sim\mathcal{G}_{q}}\bigl[D_{\mathrm{KL}}\bigl(\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid h)\|\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(\cdot\mid h)\bigr)\bigr],
``` |  | (8) |

with $`\epsilon,\epsilon_{c},\beta_{\mathrm{KL}}`$ hyperparameters and
$`\mathbb{E}_{q,i,t,k}`$ the mean over all sampled token positions of
the group. This component propagates only the outcome supervision of the
verifier; the reflection-specific token-level signal comes next.

Reflection On-Policy Distillation. To turn the sparse outcome signal
into dense supervision over reflective decisions, we condition on the
reflection meta-skills $`\kappa_{q,i}\in\mathcal{K}_{m}`$ of the
environment $`m`$ that task $`q`$ instantiates. No retrieval or extra
matching step is involved: each EnvScaler RL task already specifies its
environment, and the skill library is organized by environment, so the
corresponding skill card is loaded directly with the environment and
never depends on a benchmark answer. Prompting the same policy
$`\pi_{\theta}`$ with this skill prepended to the task turns it into a
teacher that re-scores the student rollout sampled without any skill
prior: a deterministic function $`H`$ builds the skill-augmented history
$`\widetilde{h}_{q,i,t}=H(h_{q,i,t},\kappa_{q,i})`$, and the current
policy re-scores the already sampled action token under it,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\ell^{\mathrm{skill}}_{q,i,t,k}=\log\pi_{\theta}\bigl(a_{q,i,t,k}\mid\widetilde{h}_{q,i,t},a_{q,i,t,<k}\bigr),
``` |  | (9) |

which is contrasted with the ordinary-context score
$`\ell^{\theta}_{q,i,t,k}`$ of
Equation [7](#S3.E7 "In 3.3 Stage 3: On-Policy Reflective Policy Optimization (ORPO) ‣ 3 Methodology: Agent-Reflex ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")
on exactly the same token. OPD therefore needs a single environment
rollout stream: the skill branch only scores tokens as a training-time
privileged teacher, and gradients flow through the ordinary branch
alone. Following SEED, the detached skill-induced shift and its
confidence weight are

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\Delta_{q,i,t,k}=\operatorname{sg}\bigl[\ell^{\mathrm{skill}}_{q,i,t,k}-\ell^{\theta}_{q,i,t,k}\bigr],\qquad\gamma_{q,i,t,k}=\operatorname{sigmoid}\bigl(\beta_{\mathrm{opd}}\Delta_{q,i,t,k}\bigr),
``` |  | (10) |

and we optimize

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPD}}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{q,i,t,k}\Bigl[\chi_{q,i,t,k}\,\gamma_{q,i,t,k}\bigl(\operatorname{sg}[\ell^{\mathrm{skill}}_{q,i,t,k}]-\ell^{\theta}_{q,i,t,k}\bigr)\Bigr],
``` |  | (11) |

where $`\operatorname{sg}[\cdot]`$ blocks gradients through the teacher
branch, so minimizing $`\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPD}}`$ raises the student
score on teacher-endorsed on-policy tokens. The confidence weight
$`\gamma\in(0,1)`$ is a soft weighting rather than a hard filter: it
emphasizes tokens with a positive skill-induced shift and down-weights
tokens whose shift is weak or negative.

Joint Objective. We jointly optimize the outcome-based Agent RL and
reflection OPD objectives:

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ORPO}}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{RL}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{opd}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{OPD}}.
``` |  | (12) |

The objective combines trajectory-level outcome learning with
token-level reflection supervision, further sharpening the proactive
reflection of the policy.

## 4 Experiments

### 4.1 Experimental Setups

Datasets. We evaluate our method on two groups of benchmarks.
(1) Long-horizon tool use covers general function calling and
interactive workflows: BFCL-v4 ([Patil et al., 2025](#bib.bib2)),
ACEBench ([Chen et al., 2025](#bib.bib25)), 200 stratified ToolSandbox
tasks ([Lu et al., 2025](#bib.bib27)), $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench ([Barres et
al., 2025](#bib.bib4)), and VitaBench ([He et al., 2025](#bib.bib26)).
(2) Noisy interaction uses AgentNoiseBench ([Wang et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib17)), instantiated on the $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench and
VitaBench tool- and user-noise settings. Following the EnvScaler
protocol ([Song et al., 2026](#bib.bib7)), all evaluations use the
standard MCP format and task templates, and each benchmark is scored
with its official metric.
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Datasets ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")
specifies every benchmark.

Baselines. Every trained method here, including Agent-Reflex, starts
from the same Qwen3-8B backbone under one fair experimental setting. We
compare three families: reflection methods ([Shinn et al.,
2023](#bib.bib11); [Zhao et al., 2024](#bib.bib30); [Yuan et al.,
2025](#bib.bib13); [Chen et al., 2026](#bib.bib16)), environment-scaling
methods ([Li et al., 2025](#bib.bib5); [Xu et al., 2025](#bib.bib24);
[Song et al., 2026](#bib.bib7); [Wang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib8); [Xu et
al., 2026](#bib.bib23); [Dong et al., 2026a](#bib.bib10)), and
trajectory-level RL algorithms ([Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib19); [Yu et
al., 2025](#bib.bib20); [Hu et al., 2025](#bib.bib18); [Wu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib28)).
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Baselines ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")
specifies every baseline and
Appendix [D](#A4 "Appendix D Implementation Details ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")
the implementation.

### 4.2 Main Results

#### 4.2.1 Results on Long-Horizon Tool Use.

Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.3 Stage 3: On-Policy Reflective Policy Optimization (ORPO) ‣ 3 Methodology: Agent-Reflex ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")
shows that Agent-Reflex performs well on five long-horizon agent
benchmarks, achieving the highest overall score among strong baselines.
We further make the following observations.

(1) Internalizing Reflection beyond Inference-Time Guidance.
Agent-Reflex outperforms Reflexion-8B and ExpeL-8B on VitaBench,
ACEBench, and ToolSandbox. On VitaBench, Agent-Reflex achieves 17.5%,
compared with 6.8% for Reflexion-8B. While these methods rely on
self-generated critiques or retrieved experience at inference time,
Agent-Reflex trains directly on verified recovery behavior. This may
help the policy translate reflection into corrective actions more
reliably, reducing its reliance on interpreting textual advice during
execution.

(2) Reusable Recovery Knowledge beyond Individual Trajectories.
Agent-Reflex surpasses Agent-R-8B and NoisyAgent-8B on VitaBench, BFCL,
ACEBench, and ToolSandbox. On ACEBench, it reaches 78.0%, compared with
52.0% for NoisyAgent-8B. These gains suggest that environment-level
meta-skills provide useful recovery guidance beyond individual
correction trajectories or episode-level rewards.

(3) Reflective Supervision Complements Environment Scaling. Agent-Reflex
improves over EnvScaler-8B and Agent-World-8B on all five benchmark
averages, e.g., 62.1% vs. 54.6% on $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench. On ACEBench, the
gain comes mainly from multi-turn interaction: Agent-Reflex reaches
73.3% at the turn level while matching the baselines at 85.0% step-level
accuracy. This suggests that reflective supervision complements broader
tool and task coverage.

#### 4.2.2 Robustness under Interaction Noise.

To assess whether Agent-Reflex remains effective when tool feedback or
user interactions are perturbed, we evaluate it on AgentNoiseBench. In
detail, every foundation model degrades markedly.

Generalization of Agent-Reflex to Unseen Perturbations.
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.2.1 Results on Long-Horizon Tool Use. ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")
shows that Agent-Reflex achieves the highest Overall score among the
compared 8B methods, reaching 29.1% compared with 25.9% for
NoisyAgent-8B and outperforming the other strong baselines overall.
These results indicate that its effectiveness extends to noisy
interaction.
Appendix [E.1](#A5.SS1 "E.1 Does Agent-Reflex Act Reflectively Under Noise? ‣ Appendix E Supplement Experimental Results ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")
provides a fine-grained attribution of the observed noise-robustness
gains.

### 4.3 Does On-Policy Reflective Optimization Improve Robustness?

To further assess ORPO’s effectiveness for reflection training, we
analyze along two dimensions.

(1) Performance Comparison. To evaluate online reflective learning, we
train five representative algorithms and ORPO from Qwen3-8B for 100 RL
steps on the same task pool. In
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.2.2 Robustness under Interaction Noise. ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")(a),
ORPO holds a stable advantage over GRPO, DAPO, and REINFORCE++ on BFCL
V4, $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench, and real interaction noise. The advantage also
holds against SEED, which already carries an OPD signal, and against
noisy Agent RL, so reflection meta-skills summarized from real failures
transfer better than experience estimated from rollouts alone.

(2) Training Dynamics. To assess ORPO’s stability,
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.2.2 Robustness under Interaction Noise. ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")(b)
tracks mean rollout reward over the same 100 steps. ORPO separates from
GRPO and SEED early and keeps rising after both flatten. We attribute
this stability to the confidence weighting, which emphasizes tokens with
a positive skill-induced shift and down-weights those with weak or
negative shifts, so skill-neutral tokens do not dominate the update.

Table 3: Component ablation. AgentNoiseBench averages per variant;
shading is the within-column normalized drop, so darker marks a more

Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 4.4 Ablation Study ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")
reports an ablation study of Agent-Reflex on the two AgentNoiseBench
settings. Each row removes one component while keeping the remaining
training and evaluation conditions fixed, and the complete-model scores
match those in
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.2.1 Results on Long-Horizon Tool Use. ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively").
We make three observations. (1) Removing any component degrades both
settings, showing that the components are complementary. (2) The
supervision types follow a consistent ordering: removing SR causes the
largest drop, followed by KR and UR, suggesting that failure awareness
and local repair form the foundation of reflective behavior. (3) The
skill library alone is insufficient: with the library retained, removing
OPD clearly hurts performance, while removing only its confidence
weighting also causes a decline. Thus, the gains arise from the
token-level reflection signal rather than skill exposure alone.

## 5 Conclusion

In this paper, we present Agent-Reflex, a general training framework for
incentivizing proactive reflective thinking in agents. In detail, RSD
mines reusable reflection meta-skills from matched success–failure
trajectories under grounded tool-feedback perturbations. Building on
this skill library, ReSFT turns each skill into complementary
supervision for self-reflection, skill recovery, and user-centric
correction, and ORPO further elicits proactive reflection by combining
agentic reinforcement learning under noisy interaction with
reflection-guided on-policy distillation. Across six challenging agent
benchmark suites, Agent-Reflex improves long-horizon tool use and
robustness under tool and user noise with stable training dynamics,
supporting scalable agent training.

We used generative AI tools solely to assist with literature reading and
to proofread and polish author-written text. These tools were not used
to develop research ideas, design experiments, conduct analyses,
generate results or citations, formulate survey or interview questions,
or create or modify figures. We reviewed all AI-assisted content and

and artifacts.

## Appendix

## Appendix A Supplement Related Work

### A.1 Agent Reflection Learning

Agent reflection studies how interaction feedback can reveal errors and
guide subsequent behavior. The methods differ along one axis that
matters for our claims: *where the corrective signal lives*: in the
context at inference time, in an offline trajectory rewrite, or in the
parameters.

Inference-time reflection. The first family leaves parameters untouched
and reflects in context. Reflexion appends a verbal self-critique to an
episodic buffer that later attempts read \[[Shinn et al.,
2023](#bib.bib11)\], and Self-Refine iterates generation, self-feedback,
and revision within a single episode \[[Madaan et al.,
2023](#bib.bib12)\]; ExpeL instead accumulates cross-task
natural-language insights and retrieves similar past trajectories at
test time \[[Zhao et al., 2024](#bib.bib30)\]. These methods bound what
prompting alone recovers, and that bound is informative: because the
critique is produced by the same policy that failed, it is only as good
as that policy’s model of the environment. When a tool return is
well-formed but wrong, there is nothing in the context to contradict the
failed plan, so the critique tends to restate it. Our
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.3 Stage 3: On-Policy Reflective Policy Optimization (ORPO) ‣ 3 Methodology: Agent-Reflex ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")
shows this concretely: both Reflexion and ExpeL fall below their own
backbone on the longest-horizon benchmark.

Learning from correction trajectories. The second family moves
correction into training. Agent-R combines MCTS with model-guided
selection of the revision point to construct recovery trajectories, then
learns timely correction by iterative self-training \[[Yuan et al.,
2025](#bib.bib13)\]. ReflectRL transfers reflection elicited on golden
negative trajectories into direct reasoning \[[Bi et al.,
2026](#bib.bib14)\], and LoongReflect combines privileged reflection
supervision with outcome-based RL \[[Zhang et al., 2026](#bib.bib15)\],
the closest prior work to our ORPO stage in supervision *type*, though
its privileged context is an episode-level hindsight rewrite rather than
an environment-level artifact. The shared limitation is that the
correction is synthesized per trajectory: each repair is fitted to the
episode that produced it, so nothing accumulates into a statement about
the environment that a later, differently-failing episode can reuse.

Robustness to perturbed interaction. A third line attacks the problem
from the environment side. NoisyAgent perturbs user instructions and
tool responses, mixes clean and noisy rollouts, and adaptively raises
noise difficulty, giving a complementary route to recovery and ambiguity
handling \[[Chen et al., 2026](#bib.bib16)\]. This exposes the policy to
failure states, which trajectory-level RL alone does not, but the
supervision remains a scalar return: it can express that a perturbed
episode was harder, not which recovery the specific failure admitted.

Positioning. Agent-Reflex shares the goal of learning from failure and
differs in what it learns *from* and what it stores. Before any policy
training, it consolidates cross-model behavioral contrasts (matched
success/failure pairs on the same task under the same injected noise)
into explicit, environment-indexed reflection meta-skills. A skill is
therefore reusable across episodes and mined once per environment,
rather than rewritten per trajectory. These skills then supply
supervision for autonomous recovery and user-directed correction (ReSFT)
and a privileged teacher context for token-level distillation (ORPO).
Because the skill is privileged only during training and stripped from
every stored input, inference needs no skill prompt and no auxiliary
reflector, unlike the inference-time family above, where the critique
must be produced online at deployment.

### A.2 Scalable Environment Synthesis for Agent Training

Existing approaches split into two families. The first uses language
models as implicit textual world models: Simia generates environment
feedback conditioned on tool specifications and interaction histories,
and GenEnv couples generative simulation with a capability-adapted
curriculum \[[Li et al., 2025](#bib.bib5), [Guo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib6)\]. This removes most environment-engineering cost, but
the fidelity of a simulated observation is bounded by the simulator’s
ability to keep state consistent, so long rollouts can drift away from
any realizable environment. The second family makes dynamics explicit
through executable tools, databases, and programmatic verifiers.
EnvScaler, AWM, and ScaleEnv construct environments whose transitions
execute and whose outcomes are checkable \[[Song et al.,
2026](#bib.bib7), [Wang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib8), [Tu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib9)\]; Agent-World mines databases from real service
themes, validates generated tools against them, and lets environments
and policies co-evolve through continuous task generation \[[Dong et
al., 2026a](#bib.bib10)\]; EnvACE instead internalizes dynamics by
*world rehearsal*, with one policy emitting both tool actions and the
responses they induce \[[Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib23)\]; and TOUCAN
takes a data-centric route, synthesizing tool-use trajectories from real
MCP services \[[Xu et al., 2025](#bib.bib24)\].

These efforts are why a large pool of executable environments can be
assumed today. What they do not address is the status of *failure*
inside those environments: a verifier returning zero says an episode was
hard, not which of dozens of tool calls broke the plan, what evidence
exposed it, or which recovery the situation admitted. Agent-Reflex
adopts the database-backed executable paradigm from this line and
targets that residual.

### A.3 Agentic Reinforcement Learning

GRPO removes the value network by normalizing rewards within a sampled
group \[[Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib19)\], and DAPO and REINFORCE++
improve stability and sample efficiency through clip asymmetry, dynamic
sampling, token-level loss aggregation, and variance reduction \[[Yu et
al., 2025](#bib.bib20), [Hu et al., 2025](#bib.bib18)\]. Applying these
to tool-using agents introduces a difficulty single-turn reasoning
lacks: a long episode’s return is one scalar attached to a decision
sequence of unknown length. One line of work therefore reshapes the
rollout or the credit assignment rather than the optimizer, through
hierarchical rewards with a self-critic stage \[[Dong et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib29)\], entropy-triggered partial rollouts with soft
advantage attribution \[[Dong et al., 2025c](#bib.bib21)\], and balanced
exploration across the agent and environment branches \[[Dong et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib22)\]. A complementary route leaves the reward untouched
and densifies the gradient instead: on-policy distillation scores the
student’s own sampled tokens under a teacher context, which SEED
instantiates for agents by re-scoring the same action token with and
without privileged information and gating a stop-gradient log-likelihood
shift through a sigmoid \[[Wu et al., 2026](#bib.bib28)\]. ORPO is
orthogonal to the first route and reuses SEED’s estimator unchanged in
the second; what it contributes is the content of the privileged slot,
an environment-level skill card mined once from empirical tool failures
rather than a larger model or a per-episode hindsight rewrite.

## Appendix B Datasets

All evaluations use the standard MCP interaction format and each
benchmark’s official metric, reported by domain.

### B.1 General Function Calling

- •
  BFCL-v4 \[[Patil et al., 2025](#bib.bib2)\] extends the Berkeley
  Function Calling Leaderboard from single-call accuracy toward agentic
  evaluation. We report Web, Memory, Multi-Turn, Non-Live, Live, and
  Irrelevance, and the average follows the official BFCL scoring
  procedure rather than a simple mean of the six categories. It is
  useful here because it separates call formatting from execution: a
  model can be near-saturated on Non-Live while failing the multi-turn
  categories.
- •
  ACEBench \[[Chen et al., 2025](#bib.bib25)\] evaluates normal,
  special, and agentic tool use, emphasizing when to call a tool and how
  to handle underspecified requests. We report step-level and turn-level
  accuracy, and the average follows the official ACEBench scoring
  procedure rather than a simple mean of the two; the turn-level metric
  credits a turn only when every call in it is correct, making it
  sensitive to error propagation.
- •
  ToolSandbox \[[Lu et al., 2025](#bib.bib27)\] is stateful and
  conversational, with implicit tool state dependencies, an LLM user
  simulator, and deliberately unsolvable tasks that require asking
  rather than acting. We use a stratified 200-task subset and release
  the task identifiers so the subset is reproducible.

### B.2 Long-Horizon Interactive Workflows

- •
  $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench \[[Barres et al., 2025](#bib.bib4)\] is
  *dual-control*: agent and simulated user both act on shared state. We
  report Retail, Airline, and Telecom and their macro-average. Each
  domain supplies a policy document the agent must respect, and success
  requires the final database state to match the target, so partially
  correct trajectories score zero.
- •
  VitaBench \[[He et al., 2025](#bib.bib26)\] covers delivery, in-store,
  and OTA domains plus composite *cross*-scenario tasks spanning domains
  within one episode. We report the four domains under official Avg@4
  and take the benchmark average as the macro-average of the per-domain
  scores.

### B.3 Noisy Interaction

AgentNoiseBench \[[Wang et al., 2026a](#bib.bib17)\] injects
perturbations into both sides of the interaction loop on the
$`\tau^{2}`$-Bench and VitaBench environments. Tool noise covers faulty,
incomplete, inducing, redundant, and wrong returns; user noise covers
ambiguity, topic shift, conflicting instructions, redundancy, and
boundary probing. We score with the official Stability-Gated Success
metric, which credits a task only when the whole trajectory stays valid
and therefore excludes episodes derailed by noise that answer correctly
by chance. The benchmark is out of distribution for us: our
perturbations are summarized entirely from large-scale real tool-call
failures, were designed without any reference to AgentNoiseBench, and
are injected by a different process; no AgentNoiseBench environment is
used in training.

### B.4 Training Task Pools

Two training pools must not be confused with the evaluation sets. The
RSD ecosystem supplies the SFT data: 557 Smithery-anchored environments,
each with a mined database, validated tools, executable verifiers, and
60 tasks
(Section [D.2](#A4.SS2 "D.2 Stage 1: Environment Construction and Skill Discovery ‣ Appendix D Implementation Details ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")),
from which the ReSFT corpus is synthesized. EnvScaler tasks supply the
RL data: ORPO directly reuses 2.5K EnvScaler RL tasks \[[Song et al.,
2026](#bib.bib7)\] rather than RSD-synthesized tasks, and every
algorithm in
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.2.2 Robustness under Interaction Noise. ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")
trains on this same pool, isolating the objective from the Stage 1–2
data.

## Appendix C Baselines

Foundation-model rows are reference points at a different scale; bold
and underline in
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.3 Stage 3: On-Policy Reflective Policy Optimization (ORPO) ‣ 3 Methodology: Agent-Reflex ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")
are computed among 7B–8B methods only. Most baseline results are taken
from the numbers reported in the corresponding papers. Only for methods
that are not open-sourced, or for benchmarks that a paper does not
report, do we reproduce the method locally, following the settings and
technical route of the original paper.

### C.1 Foundation Models

GPT-5.2, Claude-4.5-Sonnet, and Gemini 3 Pro are the proprietary
reference points. Qwen3-235B-A22B is a large open-weight
mixture-of-experts model included to separate scale from recipe.
Qwen3-8B is the backbone for every trained method here, including
Agent-Reflex, and is the control that matters: any margin over it is
attributable to the training recipe rather than to capacity.

### C.2 Reflection Methods

- •
  Reflexion \[[Shinn et al., 2023](#bib.bib11)\] stores verbal
  self-reflection in an episodic buffer consulted on later attempts. It
  does not update parameters, so it bounds what inference-time
  reflection recovers.
- •
  ExpeL \[[Zhao et al., 2024](#bib.bib30)\] accumulates cross-task
  experience as natural-language insights and retrieves similar past
  trajectories at test time: parameter-free, but with cross-task rather
  than within-episode memory.
- •
  Agent-R \[[Yuan et al., 2025](#bib.bib13)\] builds recovery
  trajectories by combining MCTS with model-guided selection of the
  revision point and learns timely correction by iterative
  self-training. It releases neither an 8B checkpoint nor its training
  data and does not report our benchmarks, so the rows marked ^(∗) are
  our local reproduction following the original setting.
- •
  NoisyAgent \[[Chen et al., 2026](#bib.bib16)\] trains on
  clean/perturbed mixtures with adaptively increasing noise difficulty.
  Since no checkpoint is released, its row in
  Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.3 Stage 3: On-Policy Reflective Policy Optimization (ORPO) ‣ 3 Methodology: Agent-Reflex ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")
  (marked ^(∗)) is our local reproduction following the original
  setting, and the optimization algorithm compared in
  Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.2.2 Robustness under Interaction Noise. ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")
  is likewise reproduced from the description in the paper. Its row in
  Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.2.1 Results on Long-Horizon Tool Use. ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")
  is quoted directly from the paper, whose reported $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench
  and VitaBench numbers come from RL on the evaluated domains
  themselves.

### C.3 Environment-Scaling Methods

- •
  Simulator \[[Li et al., 2025](#bib.bib5)\] is the
  model-simulated-environment route and TOUCAN \[[Xu et al.,
  2025](#bib.bib24)\] the trajectory-synthesis route.
- •
  EnvScaler \[[Song et al., 2026](#bib.bib7)\] constructs executable
  environments with verifiable outcomes and is the strongest
  environment-scaling baseline in our tables; because the ORPO stage of
  Agent-Reflex reuses its RL task pool, it is the reference for
  attributing our margin to reflective supervision rather than coverage.
- •
  AWM \[[Wang et al., 2026b](#bib.bib8)\] learns an agent world model
  over transitions.
- •
  EnvACE \[[Xu et al., 2026](#bib.bib23)\] internalizes dynamics through
  world rehearsal.
- •
  Agent-World \[[Dong et al., 2026a](#bib.bib10)\] synthesizes
  database-grounded environments of controllable difficulty over 2,000
  environments.

### C.4 Agent Policy Optimization Algorithms

These are the comparands in
Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.2.2 Robustness under Interaction Noise. ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively"),
all trained from Qwen3-8B on the same 2.5K EnvScaler tasks under matched
rollout, tool-call, and token budgets.

- •
  GRPO \[[Shao et al., 2024](#bib.bib19)\] normalizes verifier rewards
  within a rollout group and is the base of our own outcome term.
- •
  DAPO \[[Yu et al., 2025](#bib.bib20)\] adds decoupled clipping,
  dynamic sampling, token-level loss, and overlong-reward shaping.
- •
  REINFORCE++ \[[Hu et al., 2025](#bib.bib18)\] strengthens critic-free
  optimization with baseline-based variance reduction.
- •
  NoisyAgent RL \[[Chen et al., 2026](#bib.bib16)\] appears here in its
  optimization role, as clean/noisy rollout mixing with an adaptive
  noise schedule, reproduced from the paper.
- •
  SEED \[[Wu et al., 2026](#bib.bib28)\] adds same-action on-policy
  distillation to outcome-based Agent RL and is the most important
  comparand for ORPO, since it shares the estimator and differs mainly
  in what supplies the privileged context.

## Appendix D Implementation Details

### D.1 Training Guideline

Our aim is to test whether reflection can be mined, supervised, and
internalized as a meta-skill, not to maximize a leaderboard number. All
stages follow the cold-start-then-RL paradigm \[[Dong et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib29)\] so RL does not begin from a policy that cannot
complete a trajectory, and every stage and every trained method shares
the Qwen3-8B backbone, with supervised fine-tuning implemented in
LLaMA-Factory \[[Zheng et al., 2024](#bib.bib32)\] and reinforcement
learning in VERL \[[Sheng et al., 2024](#bib.bib31)\]. All RL baselines
and ORPO use the same experimental settings and hyperparameters. Tokens
belonging to tool returns and simulated user messages are excluded from
the loss; only agent-generated tokens contribute gradient, which is the
mask $`\chi_{q,i,t,k}`$ in
Equations [8](#S3.E8 "In 3.3 Stage 3: On-Policy Reflective Policy Optimization (ORPO) ‣ 3 Methodology: Agent-Reflex ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")
and [11](#S3.E11 "In 3.3 Stage 3: On-Policy Reflective Policy Optimization (ORPO) ‣ 3 Methodology: Agent-Reflex ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively");
the same exclusion applies to the ReSFT loss of
Equation [5](#S3.E5 "In 3.2 Stage 2: Reflective Supervised Fine-Tuning (ReSFT) ‣ 3 Methodology: Agent-Reflex ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively").

### D.2 Stage 1: Environment Construction and Skill Discovery

Environments. Environment topics are 557 high-usage deployed MCP servers
in the Smithery registry, ranked by the registry’s cumulative useCount.
Following Agent-World \[[Dong et al., 2026a](#bib.bib10)\], a research
agent with search, browser, code, and OS tools mines a topic-grounded
database and expands it for $`N=3`$ complexification rounds; a coding
agent then generates candidate tools with unit tests, and a tool is
retained only if it compiles, passes its tests, respects
state-transition constraints, and admits an executable verifier. Each
environment contributes 60 verifier-backed tasks. Both agents are
GPT-OSS-120B \[[OpenAI et al., 2025](#bib.bib45)\], matching the
Agent-World setting so that environment construction is not advantaged
by a stronger builder.

Failure mining and injection. Running agents across the nine public
benchmarks listed below yields 177,700 tool returns of which 24,510 are
errors. An analyzer model groups them by surface form into the eight
families of
Table [4](#A4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ D.2 Stage 1: Environment Construction and Skill Discovery ‣ Appendix D Implementation Details ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively");
the families are multi-label, so one return may land in several counts.
During construction each tool-return position is perturbed independently
with probability $`p_{\mathrm{inj}}=0.2`$ per
Equation [1](#S3.E1 "In 3.1.1 Noise-Grounded Environment Scaling ‣ 3.1 Stage 1: Environment Reflection Skill Discovery (RSD) ‣ 3 Methodology: Agent-Reflex ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively").
Both draws are balanced uniform: the family uniformly over the eight
rather than in proportion to mined frequencies, and the realization
uniformly among those compatible with the invoked tool. A clean task is
kept only if it admits a verifiable solution, and a perturbed task only
if it admits a verifiable recovery.

Benchmarks replayed for failure mining. The error returns above come
from replaying agents across nine public agentic benchmarks, chosen to
span interface types and task horizons rather than to maximize count.
Many of them interact through MCP servers or shared workspaces and
evaluate agents in those settings, which brings them close to real
deployment. The nine benchmarks are MCP-Atlas \[[Bandi et al.,
2026](#bib.bib33)\], $`\tau^{3}`$-Bench \[[Sierra Research,
2026](#bib.bib34)\], AutomationBench \[[Shepard and Salimans,
2026](#bib.bib35)\], OfficeQA Pro \[[Opsahl-Ong et al.,
2026](#bib.bib36)\], JobBench \[[Li et al., 2026b](#bib.bib37)\], Harvey
LAB \[[Harvey, 2026](#bib.bib38)\], GDPval \[[Patwardhan et al.,
2025](#bib.bib39)\], Workspace-Bench \[[Tang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib40)\], and SkillsBench \[[Li et al., 2026a](#bib.bib41)\].
Together they reach MCP servers, REST suites, retrieval backends, and
file or OS toolchains. They serve *only* as a source of observed error
returns for the taxonomy in
Table [4](#A4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ D.2 Stage 1: Environment Construction and Skill Discovery ‣ Appendix D Implementation Details ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively");
none is used for training or reported as a result.

Sampling, pairing, and extraction. Trajectories come from the nine-model
pool of
Table [5](#A4.T5 "Table 5 ‣ D.2 Stage 1: Environment Construction and Skill Discovery ‣ Appendix D Implementation Details ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")
under an identical tool-call limit, response budget, and sampling
protocol, so differences reflect behavior rather than budget.
DeepSeek-V4-Flash serves as both critique and analyzer model; together
with the environment verifier it assigns the correctness label, and
disagreements are discarded. Pairs form only within the same task, with
at least five distinct tasks per environment; the analyzer then compares
each pair and emits the environment record $`\zeta_{m}`$, from which
1,170 reflection meta-skills are summarized in total.

Training-Trajectory Sources and Policy Initialization. The diverse pool
produces behavioral contrasts for skill mining only; it never supplies a
training target. Every trajectory the policy is trained on comes from
Qwen3-8B itself: $`\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{correct}}`$ keeps only
Qwen3-8B’s verified successes, and all Stage-2 continuations are rolled
out by the same backbone. A stronger model appears solely as the
analyzer for error diagnosis and skill extraction, a task Qwen3-8B is
not reliable enough to perform. At the level of the policy that
generates trajectories we therefore stay at 8B throughout, which is what
keeps the comparison against the 7B–8B baselines fair.

We release the ReSFT and ORPO training data, the complete reflection
skill library, the Agent-Reflex-8B checkpoint, and the training and
evaluation code at
[https://github.com/RUC-NLPIR/Agent-Reflex](https://github.com/RUC-NLPIR/Agent-Reflex).

Skill record schema. A skill is a structured record rather than free
prose: a trigger over visible history with its supporting and
contradicting evidence, a diagnosis naming the failure family, a
recovery template stating when to retry, switch endpoint, ask the user,
or abort, and reversibility and partial-effect flags. Provenance and
replay-validation fields travel with each record so that a skill remains
auditable.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  Failure family |  Share |  Typical signals |  Recovery implication |
|  Server/gateway unavailable |  33.6% |  500/502/503/504 |  Retry with bounded backoff; switch endpoint after the stop rule. |
|  Authentication/permission |  17.9% |  401/403, permission denied |  Refresh credentials, request authorization, or escalate; unchanged retry is insufficient. |
|  Timeout |  14.7% |  timeout, read timeout |  Retry or narrow the request after checking whether state changed. |
|  Resource missing |  10.5% |  404, not found |  Verify the identifier or discover the resource through search/list tools. |
|  Argument/validation |  10.2% |  400/422, invalid argument |  Repair schema, types, required fields, or enums before retrying. |
|  Generic execution exception |  8.3% |  tool/operation failed |  Inspect returned evidence and choose a typed recovery rather than blind repetition. |
|  Rate limit |  4.5% |  429, too many requests |  Back off, respect quota, batch requests, or switch an allowed provider. |
|  Network connection |  0.3% |  reset/refused/network error |  Treat as transient infrastructure failure unless repeated evidence suggests otherwise. |

is the fraction of non-exclusive pattern hits over 24,510 candidate
error returns, matching
Figure [1](#S0.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")(d).
Families differ in whether an unchanged retry is admissible at all.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  Provider |  Model family |  Checkpoints for trajectory sampling |
|  Alibaba |  Qwen3 \[[Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib42)\] |  4B-Thinking, 8B, 14B, 32B, 235B-A22B |
|  Meta |  Llama \[[Grattafiori et al., 2024](#bib.bib43)\] |  3.1-8B-Instruct |
|  Google |  Gemma \[[Team et al., 2025](#bib.bib44)\] |  4-31B-it |
|  OpenAI |  GPT-OSS \[[OpenAI et al., 2025](#bib.bib45)\] |  120B |
|  DeepSeek-AI |  DeepSeek |  V4-Flash (284B) |

supplies behavioral contrasts for skill mining; all training
trajectories come from Qwen3-8B.

### D.3 Stage 2: Reflective Supervised Fine-Tuning

The three sampling strategies of
Section [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Stage 2: Reflective Supervised Fine-Tuning (ReSFT) ‣ 3 Methodology: Agent-Reflex ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")
share one actor for continuation rollouts, $`\pi_{0}=`$ Qwen3-8B, the
same backbone that is being trained, and one user simulator for UR,
$`U=`$ GPT-4.1, following the $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench setting \[[Barres et
al., 2025](#bib.bib4)\]. A sample enters the dataset only if the
environment verifier accepts the resulting episode. The final corpus
contains 54K trajectories, combining verified Qwen3-8B successes with
reflective-correction samples spread over SR, KR, and UR. Two kinds of
privileged information are kept out of every stored input. The simulator
state snapshot is used to *restore* the environment before a rollout
resumes and never appears as tokens in the context, so the policy sees
only what it would see at deployment. The skill text is removed from the
stored input in SR and KR, and in UR it never enters the context at all,
since the simulator rewrites it into a natural user message
$`u_{\kappa}`$; those synthesized user messages are retained, because a
user turn is visible at deployment whereas a skill prompt is not. The UR
simulator is prompted to cover direct correction, partial hints,
ambiguity, and deliberately incorrect advice, so compliance is not
always the right response.

### D.4 Stage 3: On-Policy Reflective Policy Optimization

ORPO starts from the ReSFT checkpoint with the skill library and
reference policy frozen. ORPO directly reuses 2.5K EnvScaler RL tasks
rather than RSD-synthesized data, which keeps the comparison against
EnvScaler and the other RL algorithms direct. For the OPD
hyperparameters, we follow the standard settings of SEED \[[Wu et al.,
2026](#bib.bib28)\] to ensure a fair comparison. Each update samples a
task group, rolls out $`G=8`$ ordinary trajectories of which a fraction
$`\nu=0.25`$ runs in perturbed environments, normalizes advantages over
the whole mixed group, and re-scores the recorded action tokens under
the skill-augmented context. The skill branch is a forward pass only: it
never queries the environment and its gradient is detached, so the
marginal cost over plain Agent RL is a forward pass rather than a
rollout. The confidence weight $`\gamma`$ is a soft token weight: it
emphasizes tokens with a positive skill-induced shift and down-weights
those whose shift is weak or negative, while every trajectory still
contributes through the outcome term. We further conduct an ablation
study on the perturbation fraction $`\nu`$. Across the tested values,
the performance remains relatively stable on the evaluated benchmarks,
with only minor fluctuations and no consistent advantage for alternative
settings. We therefore empirically set $`\nu=0.25`$.

##### Meta-skill selection and environment alignment.

The EnvScaler RL task pool is entirely distinct from the RSD task pool,
but the two are aligned at the environment level: the more than 100
environments used to construct EnvScaler’s RL tasks are covered by the
557 high-usage MCP environments collected in Stage 1. Each environment
and synthesized task is assigned a canonical environment identifier,
allowing direct lookup of the corresponding skill:

|     |                                                              |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \kappa_{q}=\mathrm{Lookup}(\mathrm{env\_id}(q),\mathcal{K}).
       ```                                                           |     |

Thus, skills mined from RSD trajectories are transferred from the
environment level to different RL tasks instantiated within the same
environment, without semantic retrieval or task-level overlap. This
directly tests the reusability and transferability of the proposed
environment-level skills. At inference time, the skill prompt is
removed, so the deployed policy does not require access to the skill
library.

### D.5 Evaluation Protocol and Contamination Control

Every benchmark is scored with its official metric under the standard
MCP format and task templates, following the EnvScaler protocol \[[Song
et al., 2026](#bib.bib7)\]. VitaBench uses official Avg@4 with the
benchmark average recomputed from per-domain scores. AgentNoiseBench
uses Stability-Gated Success, and Agent-Reflex is measured under exactly
that protocol. Following EnvScaler and Agent-World \[[Song et al.,
2026](#bib.bib7), [Dong et al., 2026a](#bib.bib10)\], every score we
measure is the mean of three independent runs, and decoding settings,
maximum turns, and tool-call limits follow each benchmark’s standard
setting. Most baseline numbers are taken from the results reported in
the corresponding papers; only for methods that are not open-sourced or
benchmarks that a paper does not report do we reproduce locally,
following the original settings and technical route.

Noise taxonomy and row protocol in
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.2.1 Results on Long-Horizon Tool Use. ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively").
Tool Noise aggregates fault, incomplete, induce, redundant and wrong
returns; User Noise aggregates ambiguity, topic shift, conflict,
redundancy and boundary probing. The Clean results of foundation models
follow the original AgentNoiseBench report and may therefore differ
slightly from
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.3 Stage 3: On-Policy Reflective Policy Optimization (ORPO) ‣ 3 Methodology: Agent-Reflex ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively").
^(∗)Reproduced locally because the paper releases no 8B checkpoint or
training data. The NoisyAgent row is quoted from its paper, which
reports only per-domain aggregates, so its two noise buckets are left
blank.

Because agent training on synthesized environments is easy to
contaminate, we state the controls explicitly. Splits are preserved at
the *environment-family* level rather than the task level, since tasks
within one environment share a database and tool set; generated
instructions and skill text are checked for near-duplicates against
benchmark instructions and tool schemas; and evaluation reference
answers never appear in any analyzer, teacher, or user-simulator prompt.
We release the task identifiers of all training data and the tool-fault
injector used during training.

## Appendix E Supplement Experimental Results

This section reports the fine-grained noise attribution deferred from
Section [4](#S4 "4 Experiments ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively").

### E.1 Does Agent-Reflex Act Reflectively Under Noise?

Task success alone cannot show whether an agent repaired for the right
reason. We therefore split the AgentNoiseBench noise settings into finer
diagnostic slices (seven tool-side and six user-side axes, which
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.2.1 Results on Long-Horizon Tool Use. ‣ 4.2 Main Results ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")
aggregates into its tool- and user-noise buckets) and score each with
the benchmark’s Stability-Gated Success
($`\mathrm{SGA}=I_{\mathrm{traj}}\!\times\!I_{\mathrm{task}}`$), which
credits a rollout only if its trajectory was never derailed by the
injected artifact, discarding turns pulled off course that answer
correctly by luck. Each axis is normalized by its own three-model mean
so noise-family difficulty cannot dominate the shape, with 95% paired
bootstrap intervals over 165 tasks per axis. As shown in
Figure [5](#A5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ E.1 Does Agent-Reflex Act Reflectively Under Noise? ‣ Appendix E Supplement Experimental Results ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively"),
Agent-Reflex leads on all thirteen axes, with the margin widest exactly
where each part of the design is meant to act.

Figure 5: Per-axis Stability-Gated Success on AgentNoiseBench’s native
taxonomy, normalized by the three-model mean on each axis (10 = that
average). (a) Seven tool-side axes. (b) Six user-side. ^(∗) marks a lead
clearing a 95% paired-bootstrap interval against *both* baselines, ^(†)
the backbone alone.

Tool side. The two axes clearing the interval against *both* baselines
are misleading lure (13.9, the largest tool-side margin) and incomplete
information (10.9), the families whose returns are well-formed, so no
schema check fires and only the evidence inside the payload reveals the
fault. This is what RSD contributes and environment scaling cannot: more
clean environments add successful trajectories, never a record of which
well-formed return silently lied. On the four hard-failure templates,
where the status code already names the fault, gains over the backbone
are uniform (12.3–13.5).

User side. The largest margin is cognitive overload (12.9), the only
user-side axis also clearing the interval against the stronger
EnvScaler-8B, and the one ReSFT’s user-reflection supervision targets
directly: when the instruction itself is the defect, the repair is to
re-scope the request rather than re-plan the tools, a behavior no
tool-side reward can teach. Pooled over both sides, Agent-Reflex is
derailed on 28.5% of rollouts against 44.8% for EnvScaler-8B and 56.1%
for the backbone. Because the metric gates on trajectory validity, none
of this is reachable by recovering an answer after being derailed: the
gains are repair, not tolerance.

### E.2 Why AgentNoiseBench Is Out of Distribution for Agent-Reflex

AgentNoiseBench is never consulted while RSD is built: neither its
taxonomy nor its injector informs our perturbations, and the two noise
designs are constructed in entirely different ways. The noise used by
Agent-Reflex comes entirely from summarizing large-scale real tool-call
failures: the eight families of
Table [4](#A4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ D.2 Stage 1: Environment Construction and Skill Discovery ‣ Appendix D Implementation Details ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")
are counted from 24,510 error returns observed while replaying agents on
nine public agentic benchmarks, and are injected into tool returns of
our own synthesized environments during construction and training
(Equation [1](#S3.E1 "In 3.1.1 Noise-Grounded Environment Scaling ‣ 3.1 Stage 1: Environment Reflection Skill Discovery (RSD) ‣ 3 Methodology: Agent-Reflex ‣ Agent-Reflex:Teaching Language Agents to Act Reflectively")).
AgentNoiseBench instead derives its categories from its own empirical
analysis of interaction noise and uses a separate injector that rewrites
tool returns and user utterances of the $`\tau^{2}`$-Bench and VitaBench
environments at evaluation time, covering seven tool-side and six
user-side diagnostic axes. The two therefore differ in their source of
noise, in the environments they act on, and in the injection process,
and no AgentNoiseBench environment, task, or injector is used anywhere
in training. Performance here therefore measures whether a reflective
policy transfers to unseen perturbations, not whether a seen noise
distribution is recalled.

## Appendix F Limitations

Our reflection skill library is mined offline from a fixed snapshot of a
large collection of executable environments. Consequently, it does not
automatically adapt to changes in tool interfaces, service behavior, or
environment dynamics. Such changes may require periodic re-mining or
lightweight maintenance to keep the library aligned with the current
environments.

Online updating, however, does not necessarily yield broadly
generalizable skills. When the available environments or tasks lack
sufficient diversity, skills summarized online may remain specific to
individual environments or local failure patterns. The broader
environmental coverage used for offline skill discovery may therefore
help explain the stronger generalization of Agent-Reflex relative to
SEED, although isolating this factor would require further controlled
experiments. This highlights the importance of balancing update
frequency with sufficient environmental coverage for skill
generalization.

Future work will investigate online skill summarization and incremental
updating across larger and more diverse environment collections,
allowing the library to incorporate new environments and emerging
failure patterns while supporting cross-environment generalization.

## Appendix G Broader Impacts and Future Directions

Scope of the current recipe. Agent-Reflex is validated on 557 executable
environments anchored in live MCP services, eight empirically mined
tool-failure families, and six evaluation suites spanning long-horizon
tool use and noisy interaction, so the recipe is exercised well beyond a
single benchmark. Its three stages are also deliberately modular: the
skill library, the reflective supervision, and the token-level objective
can each be replaced without touching the others, which makes the
extensions below incremental rather than redesigns.

Future directions. Three extensions follow naturally. First, the failure
taxonomy is textual, mined from what an agent *sees* when a service
fails; extending it to temporal signatures such as latency, concurrency,
and partial writes would widen the range of deployment faults a
reflective policy can anticipate. Second, the library is mined once at
8B scale, and testing whether it transfers across capacities, and
whether skills compose across environments rather than only within them,
would turn it from a per-recipe artifact into a reusable resource.
Third, the privileged slot in ORPO accepts any environment-level
artifact, so targets richer than reflection rules, verified sub-plans or
tool contracts for instance, can be distilled with exactly the same
estimator.

Broader impacts. An agent that recovers from failure is more useful and
also more consequential when wrong, since it takes more actions in the
world than one that halts. Our skill records therefore carry explicit
reversibility and partial-effect fields, and recovery templates
distinguish asking the user from acting unilaterally. The ReSFT
user-reflection data deliberately includes incorrect advice so the
policy learns evidence-sensitive replanning rather than obedience. All
environments are synthesized from public service specifications and
contain no real user data, and because training perturbations are mined
from real error logs, we release failure counts and families rather than
per-service identities.
````
